newsitem.title: JAPAN: Corporate Japan suffers slower profit growth.
newsitem.headline: Corporate Japan suffers slower profit growth.

text.p: Corporate Japan saw growth in profits slow in the first half of the business year, which was taken as a sign by some analysts that the nation's economy could lose steam next year.

A corporate survey showed on Tuesday that current profits at Japan's biggest companies, excluding financial institutions, rose by an average of 11 percent in the six months to September from the year earlier period. Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities. This compared with robust growth of 25 percent in the same period last year. Corporate profit growth averaged 21 percent for the 1995/96 business year ended March.

"The slower growth in interim corporate profits can be seen as a leading indicator for the overall economy, and I believe this indicates a likely economic slowdown next year," said Soichi Okuda, a senior economist at Nippon Credit Bank (NCB).

"You will see some form of a slowdown in the second half of this fiscal year, probably led by a major drop in corporate capital investment," Okuda said, who also sees Japan's economic growth rate slowing to around 1.5 percent next fiscal year.

The survey of 745 listed companies by the Wako Research Institute of Economics showed post-tax profits for the firms falling one percent year-on-year in the interim period, compared with 79 percent growth in the same period last year.
Corporate profits were supported by the weakness of the yen, which makes Japanese products more price-competitive abroad, and record low interest rates at home, analysts said.
"We saw profit increases over the past two years. In 1994, corporate restructuring efforts led to the rally, and the yen's weakness ignited the rise in 1995," said NCB's Okuda.

"But companies will enjoy smaller effects from the weaker yen and low interest rates from now on, so the tempo of the profit growth will slow to where it is more in line with the state of the economy for the full year," he said.
Earlier this month, the government raised its assessment of the economy by "half a step", painting a picture of gradual recovery following a torpid summer.
Japanese firms, hit hard by the bursting of the 1980s economic "bubble" of inflated stock and land prices, have regained some confidence, but many still remain cautious.

The Bank of Japan's closely watched survey of corporate sentiment, or "tankan", will be released on Wednesday and is expected to show big companies growing somewhat cheerier about future business, but not enough to prompt the central bank to change its easy credit stance.

"Corporate profit growth will slow in 1996/97 on fading effects from low domestic interest rates and the weak yen, but I think the underlying trend still points up," said Tetsuo Sugiura, chief economist at the Fuji Research Institute.
After slipping to a post-war low of around 80 yen in April last year, the dollar has rebounded sharply. It was standing at around 112.50 yen on Tuesday afternoon.
The yen's comparative weakness from year-ago levels has contributed to corporate profits, but analysts said benefits from such factors would diminish in the second half.

Japan's record low interest rates have helped support corporate fund-raising, but have done little to serve as an incentive for companies to raise capital investment, widely regarded as the key to economic growth, analysts said.
Furthermore, sales of goods will be temporarily hit by a planned rise in the consumption tax in April next year to five percent from three percent, they added.
Analysts said they see the country's economic growth slowing to below two percent next fiscal year after projected economic growth of around 2.5 percent in 1996/97.
